extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers evaluating or composing epic/heroic poetry (readers of Milton)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and evaluative standards for writing and judging epic/heroic poetry, illustrated by commentary on Milton's Paradise Lost; focuses on diction, description, character-consistent speech, use of classical models, and the moral/poetical effects of devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lavish diction on idle parts (Aristotle's rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet has observed Aristotle's Rule of lavishing all the Ornaments of Diction on the weak unactive Parts of the Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction should be most laboured in the idle parts of the poem; those in which neither manners nor sentiments prevail; for the manners and the sentiments are only obscured by too splendid a diction. In practice, allow florid, elaborate expression in descriptive or 'idle' passages rather than in scenes driven by sentiment or character interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify extended description by dramatic necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description of Paradise would have been faulty, had not the Poet been very particular in it, not only as it is the Scene of the Principal Action, but as it is requisite to give us an Idea of that Happiness from which our first Parents fell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long descriptive passages are acceptable when they set the scene for the principal action or are necessary to convey essential thematic material (e.g., the happiness lost). Avoid gratuitous length in descriptions that do not serve the fable or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary 'dead' nature-painting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Drawings of Gardens, Rivers, Rainbows, and the like dead Pieces of Nature, are justly censured in an Heroic Poem, when they run out into an unnecessary length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions of inert natural detail should be pared when they do not advance sentiment, character, or theme. Exception: when the setting itself is central to the action or moral purpose (see Description of Paradise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene should colour characters' thoughts and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The Reader, during their whole Course of Action, always finds himself in the Walks of Paradise... their Thoughts are always Paradisiacal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters' language, metaphors, and allusions ought to be influenced by their environment and condition. Maintain consistent sensibility appropriate to the scene (e.g., inhabitants of Paradise should speak and think with paradisiacal tones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open speeches with convincing conflict of passions
rubrics_metrics.description: This Conflict of Passions is raised with a great deal of Art, as the opening of his Speech to the Sun is very bold and noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A powerful opening speech should present internal conflict clearly and nobly, giving psychological depth and rhetorical energy (example: Satan's address to the Sun). Use bold imagery to register the speaker's emotional state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transformations and disguises to create surprise and advance plot
rubrics_metrics.description: His bounding over the Walls of Paradise... his sitting in the Shape of a Cormorant... his transforming himself into different Shapes, in order to hear their Conversation, are Circumstances that give an agreeable Surprize to the Reader, and are devised with great Art, to connect that Series of Adventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape-changing or disguise can be an effective device to produce surprise and to link episodes, but should be integrated with character motivation and plot coherence rather than used as mere contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-consistent replies and rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: His Answer upon his being discovered... is conformable to the Pride and Intrepidity of his Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure dialogue and responses are faithful to established character traits (pride, humility, courage, etc.). A character's speech should reinforce their psychology and social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebukes and moral action should be graceful and instructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Zephon's Rebuke, with the Influence it had on Satan, is exquisitely Graceful and Moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral correction or rebuke in poetry should be crafted with grace and should have plausible impact on other characters, illustrating moral lessons without descending into mere sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical borrowings are permissible when they serve the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton... fetched this beautiful Circumstance from the Iliad and Æneid, does not only insert it as a Poetical Embellishment... but makes an artful use of it for the proper carrying on of his Fable, and for the breaking off the Combat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions to Homer, Virgil, or Scripture are justified when they are used to propel the narrative, illuminate allegory, or solve dramatic problems — not merely as ornamental quotation. Use learned models with a view to usefulness in the poem's action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid small 'prettinesses' beneath the poem's genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Uriel's gliding down to the Earth upon a Sunbeam... is a Prettiness that might have been admired in a little fanciful Poet, but seems below the Genius of Milton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from trivial or overly fanciful conceits that diminish the grandeur appropriate to an epic genius. Choose devices consistent in scale and tone with the poem's ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand, divine imagery for supernatural/angelic scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description of the Host of armed Angels walking their nightly Round in Paradise... as that Account of the Hymns which our first Parents used to hear them sing... is altogether Divine, and inexpressibly amusing to the Imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict celestial or divine beings with elevated, awe-inspiring imagery and musicality; these passages should stir the imagination and convey majesty rather than bathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit speech-introductions with judgment so speech reads naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the Modern Heroick Poets have imitated the Ancients, in beginning a Speech without premising... it requires Judgment to do it in such a manner as they shall not be missed, and that the Speech may begin naturally without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dropping 'he said' or similar tags can improve flow but must be done so that the speaker remains clear and the speech begins naturally. Use omission only where context makes the speaker obvious and the transition smooth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray love with truth, sincerity, and balanced dignity/modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speeches of these two first Lovers flow equally from Passion and Sincerity... to have described the Warmth of Love, and the Professions of it, without Artifice or Hyperbole: to have made the Man speak the most endearing things, without descending from his natural Dignity, and the Woman receiving them without departing from the Modesty of her Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Love-scenes should combine warmth and truth; avoid excessive hyperbole or artifice. Preserve each character's proper attributes (dignity for the man, modesty for the woman in this context) and balance their virtues so both are admirable and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate mutual subordination of characters where thematically required
rubrics_metrics.description: This mutual Subordination of the two Sexes is wonderfully kept up in the whole Poem...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the poem's moral/structural design calls for hierarchical relations between characters, sustain that relation consistently in speech, action, and sentiment so as to support the poem's thematic architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical journal aim: expose idleness rather than excuse vice
rubrics_metrics.description: I did not design so much to expose Vice as Idleness, and aimed at those Persons who pass away their Time rather in Trifle and Impertinence, than in Crimes and Immoralities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing satirical journals or character sketches, prefer to ridicule lazy, fashionable, or frivolous behaviour (folly) rather than treating criminal vice lightly; satirical tone should illuminate triviality and affect readers' self-reflection.
